claim: The turtle visual cortex network model contains 100,000 neurons (93% excitatory and 7% inhibitory) equivalent to a 2 × 2 mm slab of turtle visual cortex.
source: The network model is composed of 100,000 neurons (93% excitatory and 7% inhibitory) equivalent, by neuronal density, to a 2 × 2 mm slab of turtle visual cortex (Figure 1A).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the network composition and size based on neuronal density measurements.

claim: Model neurons were fitted to match median membrane capacitance and leak conductance from experimental recordings.
source: We fitted membrane capacitance and leak conductance parameters to match membrane potential from previous experimental recordings under current-clamp and used the median values for our model (Figure 1B).
evidence: The manuscript describes fitting procedures to experimental data and Figure 1B shows the distributions and fits.

claim: Connection probabilities between neurons decay spatially according to a Gaussian profile fitted to experimental paired-patch recordings.
source: We fitted a Gaussian profile for the spatial decay to connection probability estimates that had been obtained from paired whole-cell patch-clamp recordings at multiple distances (Hemberger et al., 2019; Figure 1C).
evidence: The manuscript describes fitting spatial connectivity profiles to experimental data from Hemberger et al., 2019.

claim: Excitatory synaptic conductances follow a lognormal distribution fitted to experimental EPSP amplitudes.
source: We thus generated excitatory synaptic conductances in our model from a lognormal distribution fitted to the experimental data (Figure 1D, see Methods, Neuron and synapse models).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the distribution type and fitting to experimental data.

claim: Each model excitatory neuron connects to other neurons with about two connections sufficiently strong to bring the postsynaptic neuron from rest to near firing threshold.
source: Based on these experimental constraints, each model excitatory neuron connects to other neurons with a majority of weak synapses and about two connections sufficiently strong to bring the postsynaptic neuron from rest to near firing threshold (Figure 1D, inset, E).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number of strong connections per neuron based on the fitted distribution.

claim: The biologically constrained model produces reliable sequences in 94.6% of 6000 simulations.
source: We found followers in 94.6% of our 6000 simulations.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly reports the percentage of simulations producing followers.

claim: Single spikes can trigger repeatable firing sequences in cortical networks.
source: Single spikes can trigger repeatable firing sequences in cortical networks.
evidence: This is stated in the title and abstract as a main finding.

claim: Rare strong connections support sequence propagation while dense weak connections modulate propagation reliability.
source: We find that rare strong connections support sequence propagation, while dense weak connections modulate propagation reliability.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a main finding from the model analysis.

claim: Even a single spike can noticeably increase network firing rates in rat barrel cortex.
source: On the other hand, even a single spike can noticeably increase network firing rates in rat barrel cortex (London et al., 2010) and trigger reliable sequences of spikes in human and turtle cortex (Hemberger et al., 2019; Molnár et al., 2008).
evidence: The manuscript cites experimental evidence from London et al., 2010.

claim: Single spikes can trigger reliable sequences of spikes in human and turtle cortex.
source: On the other hand, even a single spike can noticeably increase network firing rates in rat barrel cortex (London et al., 2010) and trigger reliable sequences of spikes in human and turtle cortex (Hemberger et al., 2019; Molnár et al., 2008).
evidence: The manuscript cites experimental evidence from Hemberger et al., 2019 and Molnár et al., 2008.

claim: Turtle visual cortex contains only three layers and is architectonically similar to mammalian olfactory cortex or hippocampus.
source: Only containing three layers, turtle visual cortex is architectonically similar to mammalian olfactory cortex or hippocampus and evolutionarily linked to the six-layered mammalian neocortex (Fournier et al., 2015; Tosches et al., 2018).
evidence: The manuscript cites comparative anatomical studies.

claim: Activity triggered by electrically evoked single spikes in turtle cortex is reliable in three ways: responses are repeatable across trials, involve the same neurons, and respect the same temporal order.
source: Recent experiments found that the activity triggered by electrically evoked single spikes in the turtle cortex is reliable in three ways: responses are repeatable across trials, the responses involve the same neurons, and their activations respect the same temporal order (Hemberger et al., 2019).
evidence: The manuscript cites experimental findings from Hemberger et al., 2019.

claim: Repeatable sequences of spikes have been reported in rat hippocampus during replay or pre-play.
source: Repeatable sequences of spikes have been reported across various systems in vivo, such as in replay or pre-play in rat hippocampus (Buzsáki and Tingley, 2018; Diba and Buzsáki, 2007; Dragoi and Tonegawa, 2011), rat auditory and somatosensory cortex (Luczak et al., 2015; Luczak and Maclean, 2012), mouse visual and auditory cortex (Carrillo-Reid et al., 2015; Dechery and MacLean, 2017), and human middle temporal lobe (Vaz et al., 2020).
evidence: The manuscript cites multiple experimental studies reporting sequences.

claim: Around 18% of all followers in the model fall outside the frame used in experimental recordings (1.3 × 1.3 mm MEA).
source: Furthermore, around 18% of all followers in the model fall outside the frame used in the experimental recordings (defined by a 1.3 × 1.3 mm MEA, stippled line, Figure 2E, right), suggesting a possible underestimation of the number of followers and sequence length in the original experiments.
evidence: The manuscript reports a specific percentage based on model simulations and compares to experimental recording area.

claim: The model generates almost no followers when spontaneous firing rates are close to zero.
source: Our model generates almost no followers when spontaneous firing rates are close to zero.
evidence: The manuscript describes the relationship between spontaneous activity and follower generation.

claim: The number of model followers increases rapidly with increasing spontaneous firing rates, peaking at low firing rates (0.007 spk/s mean firing rate for the top 1% simulations by follower count).
source: The number of model followers increases rapidly with increasing spontaneous firing rates, peaking at low firing rates (0.007 spk/s mean firing rate for the top 1% simulations by follower count), and slowly decreases as spontaneous firing rates increase further.
evidence: The manuscript reports specific firing rate values where follower count peaks.

claim: The probability of a low-activity simulation displaying at least 1 or 10 inhibitory followers (74% and 19%, respectively) shows excellent agreement with experimental data (77% and 20%, respectively).
source: The probability of a low-activity simulation displaying at least 1 or 10 inhibitory followers (74% and 19%, respectively) shows an excellent agreement with experimental data (77% and 20%, respectively, Figure 2G).
evidence: The manuscript compares model predictions to experimental measurements.

claim: Sequences of activations of excitatory followers often last more than 150 ms and reach the spatial boundaries of the model circuit (2 × 2 mm, 100k neurons) in both low- and high-activity simulations.
source: We saw that the sequences of activations of excitatory followers often last more than 150 ms and reach the spatial boundaries of our model circuit (2 × 2 mm, 100k neurons) in both low- and high-activity simulations (Figure 2H, left).
evidence: The manuscript reports specific temporal and spatial characteristics of sequences.

claim: Inhibitory followers display near-random levels of temporal jitter in high-activity regimes.
source: Importantly, inhibitory followers display near-random levels of temporal jitter in high-activity regimes (Figure 2H, foll. jitter, standard deviation of spike delays).
evidence: The manuscript reports temporal jitter measurements from simulations.

claim: Most excitatory-to-excitatory spike transfers in low-activity simulations show a delay from pre- to postsynaptic spike of 6–8 ms, matching delays measured in turtle cortex.
source: Most excitatory-to-excitatory spike transfers in low-activity simulations show a delay from pre- to postsynaptic spike of 6–8 ms (Figure 3B), matching delays measured in turtle cortex (Hemberger et al., 2019).
evidence: The manuscript compares model spike transfer delays to experimental measurements.

claim: Excitatory-to-inhibitory spike transfers display consistently shorter delays than their excitatory-to-excitatory counterparts, even at higher firing rates.
source: Interestingly, excitatory-to-inhibitory spike transfers display consistently shorter delays than their excitatory-to-excitatory counterparts, even at higher firing rates (Figure 3B, inset), possibly reflecting the more depolarized state of inhibitory neurons (Figure 1I).
evidence: The manuscript reports differences in spike transfer delays between connection types.

claim: Excitatory spikes are rarely triggered by convergence or fan motifs but are rather the result of one-to-one spike transfers in low-activity simulations.
source: In low-activity simulations, we found that excitatory spikes are rarely triggered by convergence or fan motifs (Figure 3C, top, conv.), but they are rather the result of one-to-one spike transfers (Figure 3C, top, single).
evidence: The manuscript reports motif analysis results from simulations.

claim: Spikes from inhibitory neurons result from more spike transfers, with a prevalence of convergence motifs.
source: By contrast, we saw that spikes from inhibitory neurons result from more spike transfers, with a prevalence of convergence motifs (Figure 3C, bottom, conv.).
evidence: The manuscript reports motif analysis results for inhibitory neurons.

claim: The distribution of excitatory-to-excitatory spike transfers displays a secondary peak indicating an over-representation of strong connections.
source: Interestingly, the distribution of excitatory-to-excitatory spike transfers displays a secondary peak indicating an over-representation of strong connections (Figure 3E, top inset).
evidence: The manuscript describes the distribution of synaptic strengths involved in spike transfers.

claim: Networks with only strong connections result in very sparse excitatory connectivity, where 61.4% of excitatory neurons receive ≤2 excitatory connections.
source: We found that networks with only strong connections result in very sparse excitatory connectivity, where 61.4% of excitatory neurons receive ≤2 excitatory connections (Figure 1E).
evidence: The manuscript reports connectivity statistics for the strong-only network model.

claim: Networks with only weak connections require a much stronger drive than their intact counterparts to produce any activity and produce fewer excitatory followers (0% prob. of ≥10 followers).
source: We observed that networks with only weak connections require a much stronger drive than their intact counterparts to produce any activity (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A) and produce fewer excitatory followers (0% prob. of ≥10 followers, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C), in contrast with those with only strong connections (75%) (Figure 3F, bottom).
evidence: The manuscript compares network behavior with different connectivity configurations.

claim: Sparse connections strong enough to trigger a postsynaptic spike are necessary and sufficient to produce repeatable sequences in the model.
source: Hence, we conclude that sparse connections strong enough to trigger a postsynaptic spike are necessary and sufficient to produce repeatable sequences in our model.
evidence: The manuscript draws this conclusion from the analysis of networks with different connectivity configurations.

claim: Strong connections (in the top 0.3% of the distribution) are more frequent within than between sub-networks.
source: Across all simulations, strong connections (in the top 0.3% of the distribution) are more frequent within than between sub-networks, providing a mechanistic substrate for sub-network segregation (Figure 4E).
evidence: The manuscript reports connectivity statistics comparing within and between sub-networks.

claim: A single external inhibitory-input spike halves the probability of sub-network activation in 74% of the simulations and entirely halts its activation in 26% of the simulations.
source: We found that external inputs to gate neurons are highly effective in controlling propagation through a sub-network: a single external inhibitory-input spike halves the probability of sub-network activation in 74% of the simulations and entirely halts its activation in 26% of the simulations.
evidence: The manuscript reports specific percentages from simulations with external inputs.

claim: A single external excitatory-input spike doubles baseline sub-network activation probability in 55% of the simulations.
source: By contrast, a single external excitatory-input spike doubles baseline sub-network activation probability in 55% of the simulations (Figure 5B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The manuscript reports specific percentages from simulations with external inputs.

claim: Two randomly selected trigger neurons share at least 1 follower in only 3.12% of all tested pairs (n = 5000), and this probability drops to 0% for at least 11 followers.
source: Two triggers share at least 1 follower in only 3.12% of all tested pairs (n = 5000), and this probability drops to 0% for at least 11 followers.
evidence: The manuscript reports specific probabilities from simulations with multiple triggers.

claim: The number of followers obtained under coactivation of two triggers is smaller than the sum of the number of followers of each trigger alone.
source: The number of followers obtained under a&b coactivation is smaller than the sum of the number of followers of a and b alone (Figure 6D, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The manuscript reports sub-linear summation from coactivation simulations.

claim: Combination-specific followers represent approximately half of all followers in the coactivation protocol.
source: Combination-specific followers represent approximately half of all followers in the coactivation protocol (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The manuscript reports the proportion of combination-specific followers.

claim: Core followers typically fire early in a sequence, whereas combination-specific followers become activated later.
source: Core followers typically fire early in a sequence, whereas combination-specific followers become activated later (Figure 6F).
evidence: The manuscript reports temporal differences between follower types.

claim: 87.8% of tested contextual neurons cause some inhibition of both sub-networks.
source: Consistent with the tendency towards lateral inhibition (Figure 6D), 87.8% of the tested contextual neurons cause some inhibition of both sub-networks (bottom left quadrant, Figure 6H).
evidence: The manuscript reports specific percentages from contextual neuron simulations.

claim: About 6% of contextual neurons can determine which sub-network becomes active.
source: The small percentage (~6%) of contextual neurons that can determine which sub-network becomes active suggests a highly specific form of routing.
evidence: The manuscript reports the percentage of contextual neurons with selective routing effects.

claim: In a given trial, the path of activation through the network can be influenced by the activation of approximately 5000 contextual neurons.
source: Given the size of our model network (2 × 2 mm, 100k neurons, Figure 1A), we estimate that in a given trial, the path of activation through the network can be influenced by the activation of ~5000 contextual neurons, enabling a big reservoir for computation through routing.
evidence: The manuscript provides an estimate based on the model network size and percentage of influential neurons.

claim: Single-cell stimulation has meso- and macroscopic effects on network activity, brain state, and even behavior in rat and mouse cortex.
source: The influence of single neurons has been documented in rat and mouse cortex, where single-cell stimulation has meso- and macroscopic effects on network activity, brain state, and even behavior (Brecht et al., 2004; Doron et al., 2014; Houweling and Brecht, 2008; Kwan and Dan, 2012; Wolfe et al., 2010).
evidence: The manuscript cites multiple experimental studies.

claim: One to three spikes of a single neuron can trigger activity in the surrounding network in turtle cortex.
source: Similarly, recent experiments in turtle cortex have shown that one to three spikes of a single neuron can trigger activity in the surrounding network (Hemberger et al., 2019).
evidence: The manuscript cites experimental findings from Hemberger et al., 2019.

claim: The model predicts that followers should be detectable in experiments in vivo in the turtle cortex but mainly within the pyramidal layer.
source: Consequently, we predict that followers should be detectable in experiments in vivo in the turtle cortex but mainly within the pyramidal layer.
evidence: The manuscript makes a prediction based on model results about high-activity regimes.

claim: The model predicts the existence of sequences under in vivo levels of baseline activity in turtle cortex.
source: Our simulations further provide an experimentally testable prediction: that sequences may occur under in vivo levels of spontaneous firing rate in the turtle cortex.
evidence: The manuscript makes a prediction based on model results.

claim: In high-activity conditions, activation sequences are mainly composed of excitatory followers, whereas inhibitory followers produce less reliable and temporally jittered responses.
source: In these conditions of higher spontaneous activity, the activation sequences are mainly composed of excitatory followers, whereas inhibitory followers produce less reliable and temporally jittered responses.
evidence: The manuscript describes model predictions for high-activity regimes.

claim: Long-tailed distributions of connection strengths are found in rat visual cortex, mouse barrel and visual cortices, rat and guinea pig hippocampus, and human cortex.
source: Indeed, long-tailed distributions of connection strengths are found in rat visual cortex (Song et al., 2005), mouse barrel and visual cortices (Cossell et al., 2015; Lefort et al., 2009), rat and guinea pig hippocampus (Ikegaya et al., 2013; Sayer et al., 1990), and human cortex (Shapson-Coe et al., 2021).
evidence: The manuscript cites multiple experimental studies showing long-tailed distributions.

claim: The amplitude of large EPSPs is less variable than that of small EPSPs in rat and mouse cortices.
source: Experimental distributions of trial-to-trial variability of EPSP sizes in rat and mouse cortices show that the amplitude of large EPSPs is less variable than that of small EPSPs, supporting the greater reliability of strong connections (Buzsáki and Mizuseki, 2014; Ikegaya et al., 2013; Lefort et al., 2009).
evidence: The manuscript cites experimental evidence supporting model predictions.

claim: The distribution of synapse sizes between L2/3 pyramidal neurons in mouse primary visual cortex is best described by the combination of two lognormal distributions.
source: Recent electron microscopy evidence from mouse primary visual cortex (V1) shows that the distribution of synapse sizes between L2/3 pyramidal neurons is best described by the combination of two lognormal distributions (Dorkenwald et al., 2019).
evidence: The manuscript cites electron microscopy evidence.

claim: Long-tailed distributions of connection strengths between L2/3 neurons of mouse V1 play a prominent role in orientation tuning in vivo.
source: Interestingly, long-tailed distributions of connection strengths between L2/3 neurons of mouse V1 play a prominent role in orientation tuning in vivo (Cossell et al., 2015) (but see opposite evidence in ferret V1 Scholl et al., 2021).
evidence: The manuscript cites experimental evidence and notes conflicting evidence.

claim: In mouse V1, stimulus presentation triggers broadly tuned depolarization via a majority of weak connections, while sparse strong connections determine orientation-selective responses.
source: In mouse V1, stimulus presentation triggers broadly tuned depolarization via a majority of weak connections, while sparse strong connections determine orientation-selective responses (Cossell et al., 2015).
evidence: The manuscript cites experimental findings from Cossell et al., 2015.

claim: Lateral inhibition triggered by early responding principal neurons implements concentration-invariant coding in mouse olfactory cortex.
source: Indeed, lateral inhibition triggered by early responding principal neurons implements concentration-invariant coding in mouse olfactory cortex (Bolding and Franks, 2018).
evidence: The manuscript cites experimental evidence for lateral inhibition function.

claim: Activations of single neurons in mouse V1 tend to inhibit neurons with overlapping tuning (feature competition).
source: In line with our observation of common lateral inhibition between sub-networks (Figures 5H and 6H), activations of single neurons in mouse V1 tend to inhibit neurons with overlapping tuning (feature competition) (Chettih and Harvey, 2019).
evidence: The manuscript cites experimental evidence consistent with model predictions.

claim: The model network displays highly heterogeneous connectivity with sub-networks emerging without fine-tuned connectivity.
source: Consequently, our model displays a high degree of heterogeneity, with sub-networks emerging without fine-tuned connectivity, allowing us to make general predictions about sequence propagation and the impact of single spikes.
evidence: The manuscript describes the model's properties and emergent features.

claim: The model was constrained by experimental statistics from turtle cortex.
source: By constraining a recurrent network model with experimental statistics from turtle cortex, we generate reliable and temporally precise sequences from single spike triggers.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a key methodological approach.

claim: Applying external inputs to specific neurons in the sparse backbone of strong connections can effectively control propagation and route activity within the network.
source: Applying external inputs to specific neurons in the sparse backbone of strong connections can effectively control propagation and route activity within the network.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a main finding.

claim: Concurrent sequences interact reliably, generating a highly combinatorial space of sequence activations.
source: Finally, we demonstrate that concurrent sequences interact reliably, generating a highly combinatorial space of sequence activations.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a main finding.

claim: Sequences are composed of divergent branches of strongly connected neurons which can be selectively gated.
source: We identify sections of sequences corresponding to divergent branches of strongly connected neurons which can be selectively gated.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a main finding.

claim: The model readily generates reliable sequences in response to single-neuron activations without any fine-tuning.
source: Our model readily generates reliable sequences in response to single-neuron activations without any fine-tuning.
evidence: The manuscript states this as a key result in the Results section.

claim: Inhibitory neurons are usually activated by the convergent activation of multiple weak connections.
source: First, inhibitory neurons are usually activated by the convergent activation of multiple weak connections.
evidence: The manuscript draws this conclusion from motif analysis.

claim: Excitatory neurons are less susceptible to ongoing network activity than their inhibitory counterparts.
source: Second, we found that excitatory neurons are less susceptible to ongoing network activity than their inhibitory counterparts.
evidence: The manuscript draws this conclusion from motif analysis.

claim: Single strong excitatory inputs are the dominant drive behind excitatory spikes and the likely conduit of sequence propagation.
source: Hence, single strong excitatory inputs are the dominant drive behind excitatory spikes and, thus, the likely conduit of sequence propagation.
evidence: The manuscript draws this conclusion from motif and connectivity analysis.

claim: The model containing only strong connections often produces an excess of followers compared to the full model.
source: Interestingly, the model containing only strong connections often produces an excess of followers compared to the full model, suggesting that weak connections limit the reliability of those neurons under normal circumstances.
evidence: The manuscript reports this finding from simulations with truncated connectivity.

claim: Eliminating weak connections reduces the slope of the network's input/output curve.
source: Indeed, eliminating weak connections reduces the slope of the network's input/output (I/O) curve (Figure 3G).
evidence: The manuscript reports this finding from simulations with truncated connectivity.

claim: Eliminating weak connections causes a shift of the I/O curve to the right, increasing the range of inputs over which output activity is close to zero.
source: Eliminating weak connections also causes a shift of the I/O curve to the right, increasing the range of inputs over which output activity is close to zero.
evidence: The manuscript reports this finding from simulations with truncated connectivity.

claim: The exact spiking composition of a sequence can vary from one trial to the next.
source: As a result, the exact spiking composition of a sequence can vary from one trial to the next, consistent with our definition of followers as neurons activated in a significant fraction of, but not necessarily all, trials.
evidence: The manuscript describes trial-to-trial variability in sequences.

claim: Follower activations depend mainly on rare strong connections.
source: Because follower activations depend mainly on rare strong connections (Figure 3F), we reasoned that the activation or failure of any follower could affect the unfolding of a sequence.
evidence: The manuscript draws this conclusion from previous analysis of connectivity.

claim: Connections within each sub-network cluster are strong and belong to the tail of the distribution of connection strengths.
source: Nonetheless, when we mapped these follower clusters onto the graph of connections, we found that the connections within each cluster are strong and belong to the tail of the distribution of connection strengths (Figure 4B, right, C, right).
evidence: The manuscript reports findings from clustering analysis mapped onto connectivity.

claim: Sub-networks persist despite random connectivity without hand-tuning of network structure.
source: These sub-networks persist despite random connectivity without hand-tuning of network structure.
evidence: The manuscript emphasizes that sub-networks emerge without explicit design.

claim: At low firing rates, entropy is about 1 bit, indicating two equally likely outcomes (full failure or partial propagation).
source: The entropy is about 1 bit at low firing rates, indicating two equally likely outcomes (full failure or partial propagation).
evidence: The manuscript reports entropy analysis results.

claim: As spontaneous activity increases, entropy rises towards its maximum (2 bits), where all four outcomes become equally likely.
source: As spontaneous activity increases, entropy rises towards its maximum (2 bits), where all four outcomes become equally likely.
evidence: The manuscript reports entropy analysis results as a function of activity.

claim: The state of the network can turn on or off some sections of a sequence without altering other sections.
source: In short, despite dense recurrent connectivity, the state of the network can turn on or off some sections of a sequence without altering other sections.
evidence: The manuscript draws this conclusion from sub-network analysis.

claim: Gate neurons are identified as the neurons within each sub-network with the shortest median spike delay from trigger.
source: We first identified the gates for every sub-network of every simulation based on activity, as the neurons within each sub-network with the shortest median spike delay from trigger.
evidence: The manuscript describes the operational definition of gate neurons.

claim: Halting is most effective in a narrower time window (70 ms relative to trigger activation) than facilitation (100 ms).
source: Computing the average across all tested sub-networks, we conclude that halting is most effective in a narrower time window (relative to trigger activation) than facilitation (70 and 100 ms, respectively) (Figure 5E, left).
evidence: The manuscript reports temporal window measurements from gating simulations.

claim: The halting window appears to have a sharp temporal boundary determined by the expected spike time of the gate in the sequence.
source: Importantly, while the halting window appears to have a sharp temporal boundary determined by the expected spike time of the gate in the sequence, the facilitation window increase with increasing input amplitude.
evidence: The manuscript describes temporal characteristics of gating effects.

claim: The sub-network interactions do not follow any particular trend, suggesting that they depend on the particular realization of the random connectivity in the network.
source: The sub-network interactions do not follow any particular trend (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C), suggesting that they depend on the particular realization of the random connectivity in the network.
evidence: The manuscript reports variability in sub-network interactions.

claim: Most contextual neurons excite or inhibit both sub-networks equally (diagonal trend).
source: We found that most contextual neurons excite or inhibit both sub-networks equally (diagonal trend, Figure 6H).
evidence: The manuscript reports findings from contextual neuron simulations.

claim: Lateral excitation is present but rarer (6.7%) than lateral inhibition.
source: Lateral excitation is also present but rarer (6.7%, top right quadrant, Figure 6H).
evidence: The manuscript reports specific percentages from contextual neuron simulations.

claim: The symmetry along the diagonal is likely a consequence of random connectivity despite biological constraints.
source: The symmetry along the diagonal is likely a consequence of our random connectivity despite biological constraints and reflects our earlier observation that specific pairs of sub-networks can strongly influence each other, with the average effect being balanced (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B, right, Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The manuscript provides an interpretation of the observed symmetry.

claim: Overlap of sequences initiated by different triggers is rare but interactions between the sequences are common.
source: Together, our results indicate that overlap of sequences initiated by different triggers is rare but that interactions between the sequences are common.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes findings from multiple-trigger simulations.

claim: Sequence interactions are reliable from trial to trial: they define groups of followers that activate reliably while being specific to the combined activation or silence of multiple triggers.
source: Importantly, we find that sequence interactions are reliable from trial to trial: they define groups of followers that activate reliably while being specific to the combined activation or silence of multiple triggers.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes findings about reliability of sequence interactions.

claim: The state of just a few contextual neurons can selectively route cortical activity along alternative paths of propagation.
source: Consequently, the state of just a few contextual neurons can selectively route cortical activity along alternative paths of propagation.
evidence: The manuscript draws this conclusion from contextual neuron analysis.

claim: Cortical computations may rely on reliable yet highly specific recurrent interactions between sequences.
source: Together, our results suggest that cortical computations may rely on reliable yet highly specific recurrent interactions between sequences.
evidence: The manuscript proposes this interpretation based on model findings.

claim: The model provides a plausible circuit mechanism for flexible trajectory sequence generation observed in rat hippocampus.
source: Different replay sequences of place cells in the same environment have been observed in rat hippocampus and linked to flexible planning in goal-directed and memory tasks, and our model provides a plausible circuit mechanism for this flexible trajectory sequence generation (Pfeiffer and Foster, 2013; Widloski and Foster, 2022).
evidence: The manuscript proposes that the model mechanism could explain experimental observations.

claim: The dynamic routing of activity relies on two elements: the existence, for each propagation path, of few points of failure and specific mechanisms to manipulate them.
source: We propose that the dynamic routing of activity relies on two elements: the existence, for each propagation path, of few points of failure and specific mechanisms to manipulate them.
evidence: The manuscript proposes this mechanism based on model findings.

claim: The model never observed explosive amplification of activity despite single spikes reliably triggering many others.
source: Although a single spike can reliably trigger many others in the network, we never observed explosive amplification of activity in our model.
evidence: The manuscript reports this observation from all simulations.

claim: Multiple excitatory spikes result in a sub-linear summation of responses, likely reflecting frequent lateral inhibition onto sub-sequences.
source: On the contrary, multiple excitatory spikes result in a sub-linear summation of responses (Figure 6D), likely reflecting the frequent lateral inhibition onto sub-sequences (Figure 6H).
evidence: The manuscript reports sub-linear summation and provides an interpretation.

claim: Sequences operate in a regime where local inhibition often balances excitatory signals.
source: Together, this suggests that sequences operate in a regime where local inhibition often balances excitatory signals.
evidence: The manuscript draws this conclusion from multiple findings.

claim: The model did not explicitly construct excitatory/inhibitory balance, but lateral inhibition and routing are reminiscent of 'precise balance'.
source: We did not explicitly construct our model to display an excitatory/inhibitory balance. Still, this form of lateral inhibition and routing via the alteration of excitatory and inhibitory conductances in gate neurons are reminiscent of 'precise balance', a form of balance within short temporal windows (Bhatia et al., 2019).
evidence: The manuscript relates model findings to theoretical concepts.

claim: Reliable propagation may involve far fewer neurons and spikes than initially predicted by synfire models.
source: Consequently, reliable propagation may involve far fewer neurons and spikes than initially predicted by synfire models, with significant experimental and computational implications.
evidence: The manuscript contrasts model findings with synfire chain theory.

claim: Unstructured random connectivity in the model captures very well the experimental finding that 80% of excitatory neurons trigger sequences even when activated in isolation.
source: Interestingly, the unstructured random connectivity in our model captures very well the experimental finding that 80% of excitatory neurons trigger sequences even when activated in isolation (Hemberger et al., 2019; Figure 2G), suggesting that sparse chains of strong connections are indeed common, at least in turtle cortex.
evidence: The manuscript compares model predictions to experimental observations.

claim: A single spike could trigger multiple ones without runaway excitation, suggesting that sequences share some properties with neuronal avalanches.
source: In our model, a single spike could trigger multiple ones without runaway excitation, suggesting that sequences share some properties with neuronal avalanches (Beggs and Plenz, 2003).
evidence: The manuscript relates model behavior to avalanche theory.

claim: Criticality has been associated with the ex vivo turtle cortex after observing scale-free statistics of population activity.
source: Criticality, a dynamical regime that can maximize information transmission in recurrent networks (Beggs, 2008), has been associated with the ex vivo turtle cortex, from which data constrained our model, after observing scale-free statistics of population activity (Shew et al., 2015).
evidence: The manuscript cites experimental evidence for criticality in turtle cortex.

claim: Repeatable and precise LFP avalanches have been found in slice cultures, possibly reflecting the existence of underlying repeatable spiking sequences.
source: Indeed, repeatable and precise LFP avalanches have been found in slice cultures, possibly reflecting the existence of underlying repeatable spiking sequences (Beggs and Plenz, 2004).
evidence: The manuscript cites experimental evidence and proposes an interpretation.

claim: Network states that remain constant from trial to trial will produce sequence statistics that differ from pure branching-process statistics.
source: Consequently, network states that remain constant from trial to trial will produce sequence statistics that differ from pure branching-process statistics (e.g., powerlaws).
evidence: The manuscript proposes this prediction based on model findings.

claim: The model results suggest that some routing mechanisms might not be stochastic and operate at the population level, but rather that they are reliable and fine-grained.
source: As with criticality and synfire chains, our results suggest that some routing mechanisms might not be stochastic and operate at the population level, but rather that they are reliable and fine-grained.
evidence: The manuscript contrasts model findings with stochastic theories.

claim: Sparse strong inputs substantially affect their postsynaptic partners and network dynamics in hippocampus and cortex.
source: Modeling and in vitro studies in hippocampus and cortex have suggested that sparse strong inputs substantially affect their postsynaptic partners and network dynamics (Franks and Isaacson, 2006; Ikegaya et al., 2013; Setareh et al., 2017).
evidence: The manuscript cites modeling and experimental studies.

claim: The model was based on data from turtle cortex, yet other species may introduce variations that might be relevant.
source: We based our model on data from the turtle cortex, yet other species may introduce variations that might be relevant, including differences in operating firing rates or neuronal populations.
evidence: The manuscript acknowledges limitations and species differences.

claim: The reliability of sequence propagation may depend on connectivity features not explored in the model, such as different connectivity motifs or layer-specific connection probabilities.
source: For instance, the reliability of sequence propagation may depend on connectivity features we did not explore here, such as the presence of different connectivity motifs or differences in the distance-, layer-, and population-specific connection probabilities (Jiang et al., 2015; Song et al., 2005).
evidence: The manuscript acknowledges model limitations and cites relevant studies.

claim: The model has otherwise random connectivity beyond spatial connectivity profiles and lognormal distribution of synaptic strengths.
source: Although we based many model parameters on experimental data from the turtle visual cortex (connection strengths, single-neuron properties, connection probabilities), our model has otherwise random connectivity.
evidence: The manuscript describes the model's connectivity assumptions.

claim: Certain nonrandom features may be expected in turtle cortical connectivity, such as axonal projection biases.
source: However, other features of cortical organization, such as structured connectivity, neuronal diversity, and dendritic interactions, might affect activity propagation and routing. Indeed, certain nonrandom features may be expected in turtle cortical connectivity, such as axonal projection biases (Shein-Idelson et al., 2017), differences between apical and basal dendritic connectivity, gradients of connectivity across the cortical surface (Fournier et al., 2015), or plasticity-derived structures.
evidence: The manuscript discusses potential additional biological features not included in the model.

claim: Turtle cortex contains diverse neuronal types, as seen in mammalian cortex.
source: Transcriptomic and morphological evidence suggests that turtle cortex contains diverse neuronal types, as seen in mammalian cortex (Nenadic et al., 2003; Tosches et al., 2018).
evidence: The manuscript cites evidence for neuronal diversity.

claim: Somatostatin- and parvalbumin-expressing neurons in mouse V1 may play different roles in controlling trial-to-trial reliability.
source: For instance, somatostatin- and parvalbumin-expressing neurons in mouse V1 may play different roles in controlling trial-to-trial reliability (Rikhye et al., 2021).
evidence: The manuscript cites experimental evidence for cell-type-specific roles.

claim: Synapses may cluster in short dendritic segments to effectively drive postsynaptic spiking.
source: For instance, synapses may cluster in short dendritic segments to effectively drive postsynaptic spiking (Kirchner and Gjorgjieva, 2021; Scholl et al., 2021); these inputs may be locally balanced by inhibition Iascone et al., 2020; and sequential activation within clusters may be particularly effective at triggering somatic spiking (Ishikawa and Ikegaya, 2020).
evidence: The manuscript cites studies on dendritic computation.

claim: Most neurons in turtle dorsal cortex have receptive fields covering the entire visual field and display a wide range of orientation selectivity.
source: Most neurons have receptive fields covering the entire visual field and display a wide range of orientation selectivity (Fournier et al., 2018).
evidence: The manuscript cites experimental characterization of turtle cortex.

claim: The presence of orientation tuning in turtle cortex and the finding that excitatory neurons are mainly activated via strong connections predict that like-tuned neurons should share strong connections.
source: The presence of orientation tuning in the turtle cortex and our result that excitatory neurons are mainly activated via strong connections (Figure 3C–E) predict that like-tuned neurons should share strong connections.
evidence: The manuscript makes a prediction based on model findings and experimental observations.

claim: Experiments in turtle cortex with multiple-trigger neuron activation revealed non-additive effects on follower composition.
source: For example, experiments in the turtle cortex with multiple-trigger neuron activation revealed non-additive effects on follower composition (Hemberger et al., 2019).
evidence: The manuscript cites experimental findings.

claim: The model can mechanistically explain non-additive effects as interactions between sub-networks of strong connections.
source: We can now mechanistically explain these as interactions between sub-networks of strong connections.
evidence: The manuscript proposes a mechanistic explanation for experimental observations.

claim: The scale of temporal windows for effective single-sub-network gating is about twice as long as the standard deviation of follower spike times (approximately 100 and 50 ms, respectively).
source: In our model, the scale of the temporal windows for effective single-sub-network gating is about twice as long as the standard deviation of follower spike times (approximately 100 and 50 ms, respectively, Figures 2H and 5C).
evidence: The manuscript reports specific temporal measurements from simulations.

claim: Parallel running sequences may have the temporal precision to interact consistently across trials.
source: Consequently, parallel running sequences (e.g., as observed in the mouse auditory cortex Dechery and MacLean, 2017) may have the temporal precision to interact consistently across trials.
evidence: The manuscript proposes this based on temporal measurements and cites related experimental work.

claim: The presence of combination-specific followers suggests that the tuning of a neuron may be expressed as the result of logical operations on the tuning properties of other neurons in the recurrent circuit.
source: The presence of combination-specific followers in our model suggests that the tuning of a neuron may be expressed as the result of logical operations on the tuning properties of other neurons in the recurrent circuit.
evidence: The manuscript proposes this interpretation based on model findings.

claim: The model establishes a mechanistic link between three elements common to most cortical circuits: sparse firing, spiking sequences, and long-tailed distributions of connection strengths.
source: In conclusion, our results establish a mechanistic link between three elements common to most cortical circuits: sparse firing, spiking sequences, and long-tailed distributions of connection strengths.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes the main contribution in the conclusion.

claim: The model provides a computational interpretation for spiking sequences as the expression of reliable but flexible routing of single spikes over sets of neurons connected by strong connections.
source: We provide a computational interpretation for spiking sequences as the expression of reliable but flexible routing of single spikes over sets of neurons connected by strong connections (Figure 7).
evidence: The manuscript states this as the main conceptual contribution.
